title: Quantum Information in High-Energy Physics: a top subject
authors: Yoav Afik, Juan Ramón Muñoz de Nova
abstract: As a work selected for the Frontiers of Science Award, we present in the Proceedings of the ICBS an overview of how the techniques from the field of Quantum Information (QI) can be implemented in High-Energy Physics (HEP), including also some novel insights. We focus on the paradigmatic case of the top quark, a drosophila of a relativistic qubit. We study the presence of entanglement, perhaps the most genuine feature of Quantum Mechanics, in top-antitop quark production in high-energy colliders such as the LHC. We also analyze our experimental proposal of a quantum tomography protocol for the top-antitop quark pair, eventually leading to the entanglement observations by the ATLAS and CMS collaborations, which constituted the highest-energy observations of entanglement ever. We discuss how the concepts and techniques developed in our work have effectively spawned an already vast and rich field of QI in HEP.
summary: This work reviews the application of Quantum Information theory to High-Energy Physics, focusing on quantifying entanglement in $t ar{t}$ quark pair production at the LHC. By proposing and detailing a quantum tomography protocol, the authors connect abstract quantum concepts to concrete, measurable observables like spin correlations. The research successfully established a framework that led to the experimental confirmation of entanglement in particle collisions.
main_problem: The paper aims to bridge the theoretical framework of Quantum Information (QI) with the experimental domain of High-Energy Physics (HEP) to study fundamental quantum features like entanglement.
main_result: The authors detail how entanglement can be predicted and experimentally observed in top-antitop quark pair ($t ar{t}$) production at colliders like the LHC, leading to the highest-energy observations of entanglement to date.
method: The study employs quantum tomography protocols and diagnostic tools like entanglement witnesses and concurrence to quantify non-separability in the density matrices describing the particle pair.
model_or_system: The primary system is the $t ar{t}$ pair produced in high-energy collisions (e.g., $q ar{q}$ or $gg$ fusion) at the LHC. The quantum state is modeled using density matrices ($ho$) for two-qubit systems.
key_observables: Entanglement (non-separability), spin correlations ($\langle \sigma_i \otimes \sigma_j angle$), and the entanglement witness parameter $D$.
important_parameters: Invariant mass ($M_{t ar{t}}$), collision energy ($\sqrt{s}$), and kinematic angles ($\cos\Theta$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on leading-order (LO) QCD calculations and assumes that the measured decay lepton angular distributions can reconstruct the initial quantum state.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate Feynman diagrams for $t ar{t}$ production and show the dependence of entanglement criteria (e.g., $\Delta_{gg} > 0$) and the differential cross-section on kinematic variables.
paper_structure: The paper provides a comprehensive overview, first establishing the theoretical link between QI and HEP, then applying specific diagnostics (concurrence, witnesses) to the $t ar{t}$ system across different production channels ($q ar{q}$ vs $gg$), and concluding with the experimental realization and impact on the field.
why_interesting: The methodology of using entanglement diagnostics (like witnesses and concurrence) developed in pure QI theory to predict and interpret measurable cross-section deviations in particle physics is highly relevant for understanding quantum correlations in complex, non-equilibrium quantum systems.
